items.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
items.snippet: The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday , the FCC argues the rule will help combat an "influx of contraband cellphones" used to carry out crimes from prison. Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934 , though they're used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. "These devices [phones] are being used by inmates to order hits, run drug operations, traffic women an … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.title: Google is forcing Android app developers to properly support foldables
items.snippet: Now that Apple's foldable is here, Google wants to make sure apps on Android foldables are a good experience. Starting in April 2027, Google is going to require Android developers to make sure their apps have a baseline level of support for foldables. If they don't, developers risk not being able to publish or update their apps or have reduced visibility for their apps on Google Play. Google says Android apps must meet its "Tier 3 - Adaptive ready" standard. "Apps must fill the available display area without letterboxing or compatibility modes," Google says . items.title: Today in Apple history: Apple Park gets the official go-ahead
items.snippet: November 19, 2013: Apple gets final approval from the Cupertino City Council to proceed with building a massive second campus to house the iPhone-maker’s growing army of workers in California. Regarding the company’s new headquarters, which ultimately will be named Apple Park, Cupertino Mayor Orrin Mahoney issues a simple message: “Go for it.” However, the massive structure — with an innovative circular design that will earn it the nickname “the spaceship” — remains years away from opening, despite Apple’s ambitious schedule. Apple CEO Steve Jobs didn’t just want a bigger office for his company. He wanted a headquarters that would embody Apple’s ambitions, down to the smallest architectural detail. The sprawling circular campus now known as Apple Park was one of Jobs’ final obsessions — a $4 billion monument to his belief that great design could transform even the places where people work. Its spaceship-like ring, enormous curved glass walls and carefully landscaped grounds make it look more like a vision of the future than a corporate office. But Apple Park also revealed the contra…

And some familiar features might go away, including the Dynamic Island. Apple’s goal for the iPhone 20 seems to be to repeat what it did with the iPhone X in 2017: Lay the groundwork for what iPhone will look like for the next decade. Apple likes to celebrate big anniversaries with significant redesigns. There’s no better example than the iPhone X. Back in 2017, this model eliminated the Home button to make room for a nearly edge-to-edge OLED display. Apple also introduced Face ID along with the screen notch. Virtually every iPhone since has followed this pattern. The iPhone 20 is apparently set to do it again. Don’t expect it to be simply the current model with a faster processor. Not even close. items.title: VAST says petabyte SSDs will outgrow today’s parallel file system RAID
items.snippet: VAST Data’s Glenn Lockwood told SC26 that petabyte SSDs need global declustering plus extra parity to avoid data loss.

items.title: Phison details SSD with a built-in NPU and 64GB of memory that supports AI frameworks on the drive
items.snippet: Phison showed a computational-storage SSD with an NPU and 64GB of memory, plus Mixed Media pSLC and QLC drives, at SC26.

items.title: Jensen Huang question gets reporter ejected from Trump-Xi-Putin summit
items.snippet: Annmarie Hordern, Bloomberg's chief political correspondent and co-host of its leading program, was barred from the historic trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the U.S. after she asked the controversial question.

items.title: Lawyer’s $9,450 private AI server with 12 used Nvidia V100s now runs every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert

items.title: MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ review: RTX Spark power comes to Windows on Arm desktops, but there are trade-offs
items.snippet: MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ brings Nvidia RTX Spark N1X power to a Windows-on-Arm mini PC with 128GB of unified memory, strong local AI performance, and the ability to game on the side. But its high $7,499 price isn't that much cheaper than more versatile DGX Spark systems.

items.title: Amazon lists the Asus ROG Strix G16 at a new all-time low price of $1,179
items.snippet: Pick up a new gaming laptop for less with $575 off the Asus ROG G16 at Amazon.

items.title: Power and cooling limits force AI clusters with 100,000+ accelerators to use multiple data centers
items.snippet: Faster GPUs are no longer enough as power constraints, network congestion, and communication overhead force the industry to rethink how massive AI systems are built.

items.title: Score a huge 49% saving on a 2TB Samsung 9100 Pro SSD while you can
items.snippet: A huge discount on Amazon has brought the Gen 5 2TB Samsung 9100 Pro down to $349.99, an almost half-price saving compared to its list price.

items.title: Redditor forced to bring desktop PC in checked luggage on US-to-UK flight with GPU still installed
items.snippet: A pissed traveler decided to check their desktop CPU after a check-in attendant refused to have it carried in the cabin, despite being historically allowed by the airline.

items.snippet: Windows 0-day lets attackers run software by partially bypass the lock screen with just some keystrokes — even BitLocker-protected machines are seemingly vulnerable

items.snippet: Intel continues to reduce headcount, IT department affected this time.

items.snippet: A civil lawsuit claimed that there was "no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge about the company's illicit sales."

items.title: Get 32GB of DDR5 for $240 with this blistering Intel gaming PC bundle
items.snippet: Score Intel's latest Core Ultra 7 270K Plus with a Z890 motherboard and 32GB of DDR5-6000 memory for $240 off with this bundle.

items.title: Save 36% on this 4TB Samsung 990 Pro SSD upgrade for your gaming PC, now just 17.5 cents per GB

items.title: DDR6 RAM shrinks by 44% while delivering 4 times more bandwidth than DDR5 — JEDEC previews 12.8 GT/s modules with up to 1 terabyte of capacity per slot
items.snippet: Upcoming DDR6 memory cuts module length from 133mm to 74mm while kicking off at 12.8 GT/s, more than doubling DDR5’s baseline transfer rate.

items.title: AMD’s Twitter brag that it ‘loves gamers’ met with savage Community Note
items.snippet: Following a post on X, AMD Japan's claim that the company values gamers "above all else" saw those gamers point out that its own CEO believes the company is more focused on data centers.

items.title: Nvidia GeForce driver bug reportedly hammers SSDs with up to 30GB of writes per hour
items.snippet: Nvidia’s GeForce 621.14 and 621.24 drivers reportedly rewrite a log file nonstop, writing gigabytes to SSDs every hour.

items.title: Nvidia promises employee pay raises, equity before December to quell unrest in wake of Jensen Huang scandal
items.snippet: Interim CEO Collete Kress reportedly offered staffers higher wages and more equity on an advanced schedule at the company's first all-hands after Jensen Huang resigned.

items.title: GTA VI runs at 1440p on PS5 and Xbox Series X, but just 720p with upscaling on Series S
items.snippet: GTA VI will target 30FPS across PlayStation and Xbox consoles, with Rockstar using its own temporal anti-aliasing solution on the PS5 and Xbox Series X, Sony's PSSR 2 on the PS5 Pro, and AMD's FSR 4 on the Xbox Series S.

items.title: Nvidia says it’s ‘absurd’ to assume it predicted the agentic moment during Vera’s development
items.snippet: AMD has criticized Nvidia, and to a lesser extent Arm, for claims about creating a CPU designed for agentic AI. Nvidia is pushing back on that characterization, instead saying Vera was designed with “base principles, product intuition, and oftentimes simple allegorical laws of computer science” in a recent interview with Tom’s Hardware.

items.title: The Downfall of Jensen Huang — a timeline of allegations and scandals that brought down the king of AI infrastructure
items.snippet: Jensen’s affairs dominated headlines, but the seeds of his downfall were planted in both the bedroom and the boardroom and stretched from Beijing to Washington, with Nvidia sitting right in the middle.

items.title: Nvidia's revenue hits $115.8 billion as Vera Rubin generates $20 billion in another record-setting quarter
items.snippet: Nvidia's quarterly revenue surged to $115.8 billion as Vera Rubin achieved a record $20 billion debut, while total commitments to suppliers and customers climbed to $540 billion and rising costs prompted a revised pricing strategy for FY2028.

items.title: StarlingX 13.0 updates the network stack for distributed edge deployments
items.snippet: Edge sites do not always come with the network gear that a data center takes for granted. That’s a challenge the open-source StarlingX project from the OpenInfra Foundation is now tackling in its 13.0 update. StarlingX is an open-source distributed cloud platform that combines Linux, Kubernetes, OpenStack, and Ceph. The OpenInfra Foundation hosts the project, and operators including Verizon, Vodafone, T-Systems and KDDI use it for 5G and Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) infrastructure. Earlier this year, the StarlingX 12.0 update added precision timing capabilities to help networking stay on time. The 13.0 update tackles a different set of issues. Key features include: Gateway API support.

items.title: Sovereign AI is about control, not just location
items.snippet: Every year at MWC and other telco-related shows, I hear the same line. A new technology wave will finally let telcos create new revenue-generating services. Cloud, virtualization, software, and a number of other trends were the magic elixir that would help telcos be more than just pipes. Every year, most of them use the technology to cut costs while continuing to sell connectivity. The industry has spent two decades trying to avoid becoming a “dumb pipe,” and for the most part, it has failed.
